stem: How does a fibre-optic cable carry data?

options.content: As pulses of light
options.rationale: Correct: light travels along glass or plastic fibres.

options.content: As electrical signals in copper
options.rationale: That is how twisted pair and coaxial cables work.

options.content: As radio waves through the air
options.rationale: That is wireless transmission.

options.content: As magnetic patterns on a tape
options.rationale: That describes magnetic storage, not transmission.

explanation: Fibre-optic cable carries data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass or plastic.

stem: Why is fibre-optic cable not affected by electrical interference from nearby machinery?

options.content: It carries light, which electromagnetic noise does not disturb
options.rationale: Correct: there is no electrical signal to corrupt.

options.content: It has a thick braided copper shield around it
options.rationale: That describes coaxial cable.

options.content: Its wires are twisted together to cancel the noise
options.rationale: That describes twisted pair.

options.content: It sends data more slowly, so errors are rare
options.rationale: Fibre is the fastest cable medium.

explanation: Fibre carries light pulses, so electrical noise from motors or power lines cannot corrupt the data.

stem: What is the purpose of twisting the pairs of wires in a twisted pair cable?

options.content: To make the cable carry light more efficiently
options.rationale: Twisted pair carries electrical signals, not light.

options.content: To make the cable stiffer so it lies flat
options.rationale: Twisting makes no difference to stiffness for that purpose.

options.content: To reduce interference from outside and between the pairs
options.rationale: Correct: twisting cancels much of the noise.

options.content: To allow the cable to carry power to the computer
options.rationale: Twisting is about interference, not power.

explanation: Twisting the pairs reduces crosstalk between pairs and interference from outside sources.

stem: Which cable is commonly used to connect a satellite dish to a decoder, and has a single copper core surrounded by a braided metal shield?

options.content: Unshielded twisted pair
options.rationale: UTP has pairs of twisted wires with no shield.

options.content: Fibre-optic cable
options.rationale: Fibre has glass strands, not a copper core.

options.content: Shielded twisted pair
options.rationale: STP has several twisted pairs, not one core.

options.content: Coaxial cable
options.rationale: Correct: one central core, insulation, a braided shield and a sheath.

explanation: Coaxial cable has a single copper core, insulation, a braided shield and an outer sheath.

stem: An internet provider is laying a link between Gweru and Kwekwe, about 60 km apart, that must carry data for thousands of customers. Which medium is most suitable?

options.content: Unshielded twisted pair
options.rationale: Twisted pair is limited to short runs of about 100 m.

options.content: Coaxial cable
options.rationale: Better than twisted pair, but its bandwidth and range are far below fibre.

options.content: Infra-red
options.rationale: Infra-red needs line of sight and works over only a few metres.

options.content: Fibre-optic cable
options.rationale: Correct: highest bandwidth and least attenuation over long distances.

explanation: Long-distance, high-capacity links use fibre: it has the highest bandwidth and very low attenuation.
hints: Which medium can carry data furthest without the signal fading?

stem: Why is unshielded twisted pair still the most common cable for connecting desktop computers to switches in an office?

options.content: It has a higher bandwidth than fibre-optic cable
options.rationale: Fibre has a far higher bandwidth.

options.content: It is completely immune to electrical noise
options.rationale: UTP has the lowest noise immunity of the cables.

options.content: It is cheap, flexible and fast enough over short distances
options.rationale: Correct: for runs under about 100 m it is the sensible choice.

options.content: It can carry data much further than coaxial cable
options.rationale: Coaxial carries data further than UTP.

explanation: UTP is cheap, thin and easy to install; within an office its limited range and noise immunity do not matter.
hints: Think about cost and ease of handling for short runs.

stem: Which is a **disadvantage** of wireless media compared with cables?

options.content: New users always need a new cable run to their desk
options.rationale: That is a drawback of cables, not wireless.

options.content: Anyone in range can receive the signal, so it is less secure
options.rationale: Correct: wireless data should be encrypted.

options.content: The signal travels as light inside glass
options.rationale: That describes fibre-optic cable.

options.content: It cannot be used by portable devices
options.rationale: Wireless suits portable devices best.

explanation: Wireless signals spread through the air, so they can be intercepted; they are also affected by walls, distance and interference.
hints: What can anyone within range of a wireless signal do?

stem: A factory in Bulawayo needs a cable run of 70 m beside large electric motors. The budget is tight. Which choice is the best compromise?

options.content: Unshielded twisted pair
options.rationale: Cheap, but the motors' interference would corrupt data.

options.content: Fibre-optic cable
options.rationale: Immune to noise, but the most expensive option when the budget is tight.

options.content: Infra-red link
options.rationale: Infra-red needs a clear line of sight and works over only a few metres.

options.content: Shielded twisted pair
options.rationale: Correct: the shield reduces noise, the run is within range, and it costs less than fibre.

explanation: STP's shield protects against the motors' noise over a 70 m run at lower cost than fibre.
hints: The workshop has heavy electrical machines.

stem: Coaxial cable has better noise immunity than unshielded twisted pair cable.
explanation: True. Coaxial cable's braided metal shield protects its core from much of the outside interference.

stem: Fibre-optic cable is the cheapest and easiest cable to join and install.
explanation: False. Fibre is the most expensive to install; its fragile fibres need special equipment and skills to join.

stem: Match each medium to the statement that describes it.

right.content: Light pulses in glass; highest bandwidth
No cables; signals can be received by anyone in range
Cheap, flexible copper wires, limited to about 100 m
A single copper core with a braided shield

explanation: Twisted pair: cheap copper. Coaxial: shielded core. Fibre: light, highest bandwidth. Wireless: no cables, less secure.

stem: Match each situation to the most suitable medium.

left.content: Linking two towns 40 km apart at high speed
Connecting desktops to a switch in a quiet office
Letting customers' phones go online in a café

explanation: Long distance and high bandwidth: fibre. Short, cheap runs: UTP. Mobile devices: wireless.
hints: Look for distance, noise, cost and mobility in each situation.

stem: A school uploads a 1500-megabit video lesson over a 50 Mbit/s link. Calculate how many seconds the upload takes (ignore any delays).
workedSolution:
1. Time = amount of data ÷ bandwidth.
2. 1500 megabits ÷ 50 Mbit/s = 30 s.
hints: Both values are already in megabits.

stem: The school upgrades to a 500 Mbit/s fibre link. How many seconds does the same 1500-megabit upload now take?
explanation: 1500 ÷ 500 = 3 s: ten times the bandwidth gives one tenth of the time.
hints: Use the same file and divide by the new bandwidth.

payload.template: The amount of data a medium can carry each second is its {{blank:a}}. The weakening of a signal as it travels along a cable is called {{blank:b}}. Unwanted signals that corrupt data are called {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Bandwidth: data per second. Attenuation: signal weakening. Noise (interference): unwanted signals.

stem: Give **two** reasons why fibre-optic cable is used for links between towns instead of twisted pair.

points.description: Fibre carries data over long distances with little attenuation (twisted pair is limited to short runs)
Fibre has a much higher bandwidth / is immune to electrical interference

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Fibre carries light many kilometres without the signal fading, whereas twisted pair only works up to about 100 m, and fibre has a far higher bandwidth for thousands of users.

explanation: Fibre's low attenuation, high bandwidth and immunity to electrical noise suit long links.
hints: One point about distance, one about interference or bandwidth.

stem: A secondary school in Masvingo is equipping a new library with 15 desktop computers and wants learners to use their tablets there too. Recommend media for the library and justify your answer.

points.description: Twisted pair (UTP) cable for the desktops
because the desktops stay in one place, and cable is cheap, faster and more secure over short distances
Wireless (Wi-Fi) for the tablets, because they move about and have no network port

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Connect the 15 desktops with twisted pair to a switch, because they never move and cable is cheap, fast and harder to intercept over these short runs. Add a Wi-Fi access point for the tablets, because they are carried around and cannot plug in.

explanation: Fixed devices suit cheap, fast cable; mobile devices need wireless.
hints: Think about cost, mobility, speed and security.

stem: A sugar estate near Chiredzi has a head office and a mill 2 km apart. The mill has large electric motors. The estate also wants internet access for workers' phones in the canteen.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which medium should link the head office to the mill?

options.content: Unshielded twisted pair
options.rationale: Too short a range and poor noise immunity.

options.content: Fibre-optic cable
options.rationale: Correct: long distance, high bandwidth, immune to the motors' noise.

options.content: Bluetooth
options.rationale: Bluetooth reaches only about 10 m.

options.content: Infra-red
options.rationale: Infra-red works only over a few metres in line of sight.

parts.explanation: Fibre: long range, high bandwidth, no electrical interference.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the motors at the mill make unshielded twisted pair unsuitable there.

points.description: which corrupts the electrical signals in unshielded copper wires (causing errors and retransmissions)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Large motors give off electromagnetic interference, and unshielded copper picks it up, so the data would be corrupted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: A 900-megabit backup file is sent from the mill to head office over a 300 Mbit/s link. How many seconds does it take?

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using wireless media in the canteen.

points.description: Advantage: workers' phones connect without cables / many users can join easily
Disadvantage: lower security (signals can be intercepted) / bandwidth shared between users / affected by walls and interference

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Phones can connect without any cables, but the signal can be picked up by anyone in range, so it must be encrypted.

hints: Match each medium to distance, noise and cost.

stem: Nyasha is advising a small internet café in Mutare that is replacing its old coaxial cabling.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Coaxial cable is thinner and more flexible than twisted pair cable.
parts.explanation: False. Coaxial is thicker and stiffer than twisted pair.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each feature to the medium that has it.

left.content: Copper core inside a braided shield

parts.explanation: Twisted pair is cheapest; fibre is immune to electrical noise; coaxial has a shielded core.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Compare twisted pair and fibre-optic cable for the café's 20 computers, which are all within 30 m of the switch. Recommend one.

points.description: Twisted pair is much cheaper and easier to install/join
Fibre has higher bandwidth / is immune to interference / carries data further
Within 30 m, twisted pair's range and bandwidth are enough
Recommends twisted pair for the café (or fibre with a justified reason)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Twisted pair costs far less and is easy to cut and fit, while fibre gives more bandwidth, longer range and immunity to interference. All the computers are within 30 m, well inside twisted pair's range, and a café does not need fibre's speed to each desk, so twisted pair is the sensible choice.

hints: Compare the cables on at least two features.
Coaxial is between twisted pair and fibre on most features.
